transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I decided to come in because... what really scared me enough to finally ask for help is that I keep having these mornings where I think it might just be easier if I didn't wake up. I mean, I don't have a plan to actually hurt myself or anything like that, but having that thought so often... it made me realize I needed to talk to someone.
How long have you been having these thoughts about it being easier not to wake up? Are we talking days, weeks, or months?
It's been about a month. They started right after my sister died... it was very unexpected. So, yes, I'd say it's been going on for about four weeks now.

Besides these thoughts about not waking up, have you noticed other changes in yourself over this past month—such as difficulty sleeping, loss of interest in things you normally enjoy, or feeling persistently sad or empty throughout the day?

Well, the sadness is definitely there, pretty much all the time since she passed. But I think the hardest part is that I've lost the joy in things I usually love. I still make myself go to my book club and the community dance night, but... I just sit there feeling like I'm behind a pane of glass. Like I'm not really part of it. And even at home, my garden and cooking for the neighbors used to give me a nice little lift, but lately, I just don't feel anything from it at all.

Before your sister passed away, had you ever experienced a period like this—where you felt persistently sad, lost interest in things you enjoyed, or had thoughts about not wanting to be alive—even for a few weeks at a time?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've been sad before, of course—when my parents passed, or when I retired and had to adjust to not working anymore. But it was never like this. I always still wanted to be here, and I could still find things to look forward to. This is... this is the first time I've ever felt this empty for this long.

Besides your sister's death, has anything else significant or stressful happened in your life around the time these feelings started, or do you feel like your sister's passing is the main reason for how you're feeling right now?

No, I don't think so. There really hasn't been anything else... my life has been pretty quiet and steady otherwise. I really do feel like losing her so suddenly is the main reason I'm feeling this way. It's the only major thing that's happened.

When you think about how you're feeling right now—the emptiness, the loss of joy, the thoughts about not waking up—does this feel like a natural response to losing your sister, or does it feel like something more than what you would have expected yourself to experience after such a loss?

Well, I'm honestly not sure. I mean... I expected to be terribly sad, of course. Losing her was a huge blow. But I've never been through a loss quite like this, so I don't really know what's considered a natural response. 

I didn't expect to feel quite this empty, or to have those thoughts about just not waking up... but whether that's just a normal part of this kind of grief or if it's something more, I really couldn't say. I just know it feels very heavy.

When you think about your sister and her death, does that thought trigger most of your sadness and emptiness, or do you find yourself feeling this heavy emptiness and lack of joy throughout the day even when you're not actively thinking about her?

I think it's just there all the time. I mean, thinking about her definitely makes it sharper, or worse, I guess... but even when I'm trying to distract myself or just going about my day, that heavy feeling is still sitting with me. 

It's not like I feel fine until I remember she's gone. The emptiness is just sort of... always in the background, whether I'm actively thinking about her or not.

Over this past month, have you noticed changes in your sleep—like sleeping much more than usual, or having trouble staying asleep? And separately, have you noticed changes in your appetite or energy levels?

My sleep has definitely been off. I don't really sleep through the night anymore. I fall asleep in bits and pieces, just sort of dozing, and then I wake up way before dawn. My mind just starts turning right away, and I usually can't get settled or fall back asleep before the day actually starts. 

As for my energy... well, it's pretty low. I just don't have the drive to do much. And my appetite hasn't been great either. I eat because I know I need to, but I'm not really hungry or interested in food lately.

If your sister hadn't died, do you think you'd be experiencing this same level of emptiness, lack of interest in things, sleep problems, and low energy right now—or do you feel these symptoms are directly tied to her death and wouldn't be happening otherwise?

I really don't know. I mean, I suppose it's possible I'd be feeling this way anyway, but... it's hard to separate it all out. Her death was such a big event, it's hard to imagine what my life would look like right now if it hadn't happened. I just know that this is how I feel right now, and it's been going on since she passed. I can't really say for sure what would be happening if things were different.

Before your sister passed away, would you describe yourself as generally being a person with good energy and motivation, or have you struggled with low energy and lack of motivation even during normal, peaceful times in your life?

I've always been pretty active, really. Before all this happened, I had good energy. I'd keep busy around the house, see friends, just do normal things without really having to push myself to do them. I wouldn't say I struggled with low motivation or anything like that during regular times. This feeling of just having no drive... this is new.

On a typical day over this past month, roughly how many hours would you say you're experiencing that heavy, empty feeling—is it pretty much all day long, or are there significant parts of the day where you feel a bit lighter or more like yourself?

I haven't really kept track of the hours, to be honest. It's... well, I'm not really sure how to measure it. 

It just feels like it's there most of the day, kind of hanging over me. I mean, there might be moments where I'm a little distracted by something around the house, and maybe it doesn't feel quite as heavy right in that exact moment, but... I wouldn't say I ever really feel like my normal self. It's just sort of a constant background feeling, so it's hard to put a specific number on it.

When you wake up in the morning, how long does it typically take before you start to feel that heavy, empty feeling—does it hit you right away, or do you have an hour or two where you might feel a bit more okay before it settles in?

It usually hits me right away. I mean, as soon as I open my eyes and realize I'm awake, it's just... there. I don't really get a break in the mornings. It's like I wake up tired and heavy, and I just want to pull the covers back over my head. There's no hour or two of feeling okay first.

When you're doing something that you know is important or meaningful—like visiting with a close friend or working on something you care about—does that activity provide any temporary relief from the heavy feeling, or does the emptiness persist even during those moments?

I still try to make myself show up for things, like my book club or the dance night I usually go to. But lately, I just sit there feeling like... like I'm behind a pane of glass. Even the things I really care about, like my garden or cooking for the neighbors, they just don't give me that little lift they used to. The emptiness is just still there.

Over this past month, have there been any days or moments—even brief ones—where you felt a genuine sense of relief, comfort, or a lightening of that heavy feeling, perhaps when you were with someone you're very close to or doing something particularly meaningful?

No, I... I really haven't. Like I mentioned a moment ago, even when I'm around my close friends or doing things I usually care about, it doesn't really lift. I haven't noticed any days this past month where I felt a real sense of relief or comfort from it. It just sort of stays with me, no matter what I'm doing.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a one-month history of persistent depressed mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, appetite loss, low energy, and passive suicidal ideation following her sister's unexpected death. While the symptoms are temporally related to a significant psychosocial stressor (bereavement), the pervasive nature of the depressive symptoms—present throughout the day regardless of context, unresponsive to meaningful activities, with morning onset and no periods of relief—meets criteria for Major Depressive Disorder. The severity and persistence of symptoms, including the emergence of suicidal ideation (a feature not typically expected in uncomplicated grief), warrants diagnosis of F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, unspecified severity) rather than a grief-related adjustment disorder.

confirmed_symptoms: Persistent sadness present almost all the time since sister's death
Heavy, empty feeling present throughout the day, even when not actively thinking about sister
Immediate onset of heavy feeling upon waking each morning
Loss of joy in previously enjoyed activities (book club, community dance, gardening, cooking)
Feels 'behind a pane of glass' at social activities despite attendance
No genuine relief or lightening of mood even during meaningful activities or time with close friends
No days or moments of relief or comfort experienced in past month
Sleep fragmentation with early morning awakening before dawn
Difficulty falling back asleep after early waking
Mind racing upon waking, unable to settle
Reduced appetite with eating only out of necessity rather than hunger
Persistently low energy and lack of drive
Recurrent thoughts that it might be easier not to wake up
Passive suicidal ideation occurring frequently in mornings
No active plan or intent, but ideation significant enough to prompt seeking help

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Symptoms present for approximately one month (four weeks) since sister's unexpected death
additional_requirements: Onset clearly temporally related to significant psychosocial stressor (sister's sudden death)
No prior history of similar depressive episodes despite previous losses (parents' deaths, retirement adjustment)
Pre-morbid functioning characterized by good energy, motivation, and active engagement
Symptoms represent a clear change from baseline functioning
Depressive symptoms pervasive and unresponsive to context or meaningful engagement
